papers.title: Syringe reuse in HCV transmission among people who inject drugs: behavioral thresholds and optimal control
papers.abstract: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) transmission among people who inject drugs (PWID) is driven largely by syringe sharing and reuse, yet existing models rarely treat reuse as a behavior that individuals adopt and abandon. In this work, we develop and analyze a four-compartment epidemic model that explicitly incorporates syringe reuse as a distinct behavioral process, introducing a high-risk susceptible subgroup that acquires infection through both direct contact and syringe-mediated transmission. We establish the well-posedness and biological feasibility of the model, derive the basic reproduction number, and analyze the existence and stability of the disease-free and endemic equilibria along with closed-form behavioral threshold conditions for syringe-reuse adoption and cessation. Global sensitivity and scenario analyses reveal that while transmission and recovery parameters dominate epidemic potential, behavioral parameters governing the adoption and cessation of syringe reuse play a crucial role in disease persistence and control thresholds. The model's projected infection dynamics are broadly consistent with observed U.S. HCV incidence trends. We further formulate an optimal control problem targeting reuse initiation and cessation, and show through cost-effectiveness analysis that combined behavioral interventions outperform single-component strategies in reducing both infection and high-risk behavior. These results indicate that behavioral prevention aimed at syringe reuse is a necessary component of sustained HCV control among PWID.

papers.title: Electrical grid stabilisation through agent strategies : a mean-field game approach
papers.abstract: We propose and solve a minimal model based on mean-field game theory to study decentralized power consumption strategies to stabilize power grids. The mean-field Kuramoto description of an electrical network is coupled to agents with anticipatory capacity for decision making in energy consumption. Each agent minimizes an individual cost which includes both a financial part (cost induce by consumption and by power reservation) imposed by a central authority, and a (personal) non-monetary part. This elementary model of active oscillators is exactly solvable in the steady state regime. We show that the synchronized regime of the network can be significantly extended by the game.

papers.title: Source Detection in Complex Networks: Observability, Identifiability, and Inference Frameworks
papers.abstract: Tracing diffusion to its origin is a central inverse problem in complex networks, with applications ranging from epidemic investigation and information spreading to cyber incidents and disruptions in interconnected systems. Although source-detection methods have advanced along diverse methodological lines, their capabilities cannot be assessed independently of the evidence on which they operate. Network structure and diffusion dynamics determine which propagation histories are possible, while the observation mechanism determines which traces of those histories are retained. This review develops an information-centric and identifiability-aware perspective that connects these elements to source inference. We organize existing research around three overlapping observation settings: complete state snapshots, incomplete or noisy observations, and sensor-based observation and design. Within this organization, we examine structural, probabilistic, message-passing, simulation-based, and learning-based methods, comparing their required inputs, underlying assumptions, inference mechanisms, and computational demands. System-theoretic observability, statistical identifiability, and information-theoretic constraints provide complementary ways to examine what the available observations can reveal, while separating limitations of the evidence from those of estimation. Drawing on applications across epidemiological, information, biological, neural, and socioeconomic systems, we identify challenges in uncertainty assessment, model robustness, transfer across networks, and the acquisition of informative observations. This synthesis clarifies the conditions under which diffusion sources can be identified and how inference methods should be selected according to the available observations.

papers.title: How Many Keys Must a Quantum Computer Break to Take Over a Blockchain? A Quantum Nakamoto Coefficient for Fifteen Proof-of-Stake Networks
papers.abstract: Blockchains that run on proof of stake, among them Ethereum and Solana, are secured by a vote: a transaction becomes irreversible once computers holding two thirds of the deposited money have signed it. Each signature is made with a secret key whose public counterpart is permanently visible, and a large quantum computer could compute the secret from the public key. We ask a simple question: how many such keys would it have to break to take over the vote? We call the answer the quantum Nakamoto coefficient and measure it on live data from fifteen networks, collected on 15 November 2026. For fourteen of them, 2 to 18 keys are enough to break the network's security guarantee and 7 to 77 to control it outright; at one key every 12 minutes, the pace implied by recent resource estimates, a single quantum computer would defeat the guarantee of any of these networks in less than four hours and take full control in less than sixteen hours. Ethereum is far more robust, but a 2025 change that lets operators merge their deposits into fewer keys has cut the number of keys at its first threshold from about 465,000 to 7,682, a factor of 60. We derive a simple formula for this effect, and another for the small rotating committee on which wallets rely, and confirm both on the data. For fourteen of the fifteen networks, the first large quantum computer would be less than a day away from total control. Their validator signatures should therefore be migrated to post-quantum schemes before such a machine exists, since once it does, the time to respond is measured in hours.

papers.title: The Phases of Hierarchy
papers.abstract: We develop a dynamical phase theory of hierarchy, in which depth decides whether a population of size $N$ that revises its own environment can correct it without overcorrecting. The statistics that let a large majority detect a small bias - the basis of the Condorcet jury theorem - also make its response grow as $\sqrt{N}$. Fed back into the environment it is judging, this sharpening destabilises the matched state through a flip bifurcation at a critical loop gain, which we obtain analytically for a class of models we term adaptive normal forms. We show that this instability can be attenuated by hierarchical layering, requiring a depth scaling logarithmically with $N$. This recovers known logarithmic bounds in organisational economics directly from dynamic stability conditions. Hierarchical depth carries its own costs however, and by analysing the signal chain transmission up the hierarchy we show that beyond a finite depth no correction reaches the top before its deadline, and that below it the cost of arrival grows exponentially with depth. A hierarchy that is too flat therefore oscillates and one that is too deep cannot be steered in time, leaving a bounded window of depth between an unstable flat phase and a frozen inertial phase. We further show that these results can be generalised by treating each layer as a real-space renormalisation step, classifying aggregation rules by how they transmit bias. This establishes a connection between these dynamic results to attention in Transformers, where a residual update is diffusion on the token graph and depth plays the role of scale. Finally we show these phase boundaries are observable in finite sampling, and propose measurements which may characterise the proposed phases in real adaptive systems.

papers.title: Funding Landscape of Early-Career Scientists: A Perspective from the AGU SPA Early Career Leadership Advisory Committee
papers.abstract: Like researchers across many scientific fields, early-career researchers in heliophysics face a critical transition from supervised research to independent scientific inquiry. However, the funding landscape that should support this transition is fragmented and unpredictable. Here we examine the current funding opportunities available to early-career researchers in heliophysics alongside the historical experiences of established scientists who navigated similar transitions. We catalog the major U.S. federal programs targeting early-career space physicists, documenting their eligibility constraints, selection rates, and accessibility. Access varies with career stage, appointment type, citizenship requirements, and solicitation schedules, and selection rates can swing sharply: the NASA Heliophysics Early Career Investigator Program (ECIP) selected 28% of proposals in 2022 but only 6% in 2024. To provide historical context, we collected survey responses from 30 researchers whose PhDs span 1972-2016 and conducted eight interviews with mid- and senior-career researchers. Most respondents viewed the present funding environment as more difficult than their own early careers, identifying predictability of opportunity, not ease, as what enabled earlier generations to build independence. Salary support alone does not guarantee opportunities to develop scientific leadership; accessible PI awards and real responsibility within collaborative projects can both contribute to that development. We recommend predictable, adequately sized grant programs for early-career principal investigators, transparent reporting of selection statistics across all early-career programs, continued use of dual-anonymous peer review, and named leadership roles for early-career researchers within large projects.

papers.title: The Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model: A Semi-mechanistic Generative Model for Temporal Hypergraphs
papers.abstract: Many complex networks involve time-varying relations between more than two nodes. Such networks are naturally modeled by temporal hypergraphs. We propose the Hawkes Hypergraph Copy Model (HHCM), a semi-mechanistic model for temporal hypergraphs that combines a Hawkes process to model the timestamps of hyperedges with a noisy copy mechanism to model the nodes present in hyperedges. Each hyperedge is either generated as an exogenous event with a baseline rate or an endogenous event as a noisy copy of a previous hyperedge. Our proposed model can be used for credit attribution, where the objective is to quantify the influence or contribution of a prior hyperedge to a current one. We apply the HHCM to perform attribution on several real network datasets with higher-order relations, including email networks and militarized interstate dispute networks.
